title: Touch-move and the chess clock
summary: The over-the-board rules that cost club players games: touch-move, adjusting, one-hand moves, and how the clock, increment and delay work.

steps.md:
Online, a misclick is the only accident. Over the board, **touching is committing**. If it is your move and you deliberately touch one of your pieces, you must move it (if it has a legal move). Touch an opponent's piece and you must capture it (if you can). To straighten a piece, say **"I adjust"** (or "j'adoube") *before* touching it.

A move is complete when you **release** the piece on its new square. Then press the clock **with the same hand** you moved with.

steps.question: It is your move. Without saying anything, you pick up your bishop, realise it is a bad idea, and put it back. What now?
choices: Nothing: you put it back on its original square
You must move that bishop if it has any legal move
You receive a warning and may play any move
Your opponent chooses which piece you must move
steps.explain: Art. 4.3: a deliberately touched own piece must be moved, provided it has a legal move. Putting it back changes nothing. Only if the touched piece has no legal move may you play any move (Art. 4.5).

steps.prompt: Touch-move in practice: you (Black) reached for your f8-bishop without saying "I adjust". You must now move that bishop. Pick its best square.
steps.explain: Bc5 develops actively and eyes f2. ...Be7 is also playable, but once the bishop is touched you only get to choose *where* it goes, so make it the most active square. The lesson: decide before your hand moves.
steps.hint: The bishop wants the most active diagonal available.

steps.question: Your opponent touches their queen, then says "I adjust" and plays a knight move instead. What is the correct reaction?
choices: Accept it: "I adjust" can be said at any time
Claim touch-move before you touch any piece yourself; the queen must be moved if it can
Stop the clock and ask the arbiter to award you the game
Touch-move is only enforced in rapid games
steps.explain: Saying "I adjust" only works *before* touching. Claim immediately: you lose the right to claim once you deliberately touch a piece yourself (Art. 4.8). Stop the clock and call the arbiter if your opponent disagrees.

steps.question: Which castling execution is legal over the board?
choices: Move the rook first, then the king
Move king and rook at the same time with both hands
Move the king two squares first, then the rook, with one hand
Move the king one square, press the clock, then finish castling
steps.explain: Castling is a king move: touch the king first and move it two squares, then move the rook with the same hand. Touching the rook first means a rook move (Art. 4.4.2). Using two hands is treated as an illegal move (Art. 7.5.4).

steps.md: **The clock.** Each player has a time budget. Common controls: classical (60+ minutes), rapid (more than 10 and less than 60 minutes), blitz (10 minutes or less). **Increment** (Fischer) adds time after every move (e.g. 15+10 adds 10 seconds per move). **Delay** (Bronstein / US) counts down a few seconds before your main time starts running. The flag falling means a loss, unless your opponent cannot possibly checkmate you.

steps.question: A game is played at 15+10. You have 40 seconds left and make a move quickly in 4 seconds. How much time do you have after pressing the clock?
choices: 36 seconds
46 seconds
50 seconds
40 seconds
steps.explain: Increment is added after each completed move: 40 - 4 + 10 = 46 seconds. In increment games you can survive time trouble indefinitely if you move faster than the increment.

steps.question: Under FIDE rules, which of these is a rapid time control?
steps.explain: Rapid is more than 10 and less than 60 minutes per player, where the increment counts x60 (App. A.1). 15+10 = 15 + 10 = 25-minute equivalent. 5+3 and 10+0 are blitz; 90+30 is classical.

steps.question: Your opponent's flag falls. You have only a bare king left. What is the result?
choices: You win on time
Draw: you cannot checkmate by any legal series of moves
Your opponent loses only if you claim within 10 seconds
The game continues with 2 minutes added
steps.explain: Flag fall loses, except when the opponent cannot checkmate by any legal sequence; then it is a draw (Art. 6.9). A lone king can never mate.

steps.question: Retrieval check: which three habits avoid most over-the-board rule accidents?
choices: Say "I adjust" before straightening; decide fully before touching; press the clock with the moving hand
Always touch the rook first when castling; use both hands in time trouble; stop the clock to think
Adjust pieces on your opponent's time; touch pieces to help visualise; press with either hand
Only claim touch-move after the game; ignore the clock until move 40; castle with two hands
steps.explain: Adjust only with an announcement, think with your hands off the pieces, and use one hand for both the move and the clock.

sources: FIDE Laws of Chess (2023) Art. 4.1-4.8, 6.1-6.12, App. A.1, B.1
